question: What is IBM Guardium Data Protection and what are its core components?
answer: IBM Guardium Data Protection (GDP) is a database activity monitoring (DAM) platform that provides real-time visibility and protection for sensitive data in databases. Its core components are: (1) Collector — deployed near database servers, captures all database traffic via S-TAP agents, exposes REST API on port 8443 and SSH CLI on port 16022; (2) Aggregator — consolidates data from multiple Collectors for centralised reporting and policy management; (3) Central Manager — manages multiple Aggregators and Collectors at enterprise scale; (4) S-TAP — a software tap agent installed on the database server that captures traffic at the OS level and reports to the Collector on TCP 8075; (5) GIM (Guardium Installation Manager) — IBM's enterprise tool for centralised S-TAP lifecycle management, with REST API on TCP 8082.

question: What REST API endpoint registers a Guardium Collector to an Aggregator?
answer: To register a Guardium Collector to an Aggregator, send a POST request to /restAPI/register_aggregator on the Collector's REST API endpoint (https://<collector-ip>:8443/restAPI/register_aggregator). The JSON payload must include: aggregatorIP (the Aggregator's IP address), aggregatorUsername (admin username on the Aggregator), and aggregatorPassword (admin password on the Aggregator). After submitting, poll GET /restAPI/aggregator_registration_status on the Collector until the status field returns 'registered'. You can then verify via GET /restAPI/managed_units on the Aggregator to confirm the Collector appears in the managed units list.

question: How do you install S-TAP on a Linux database server?
answer: To install S-TAP on a Linux database server: (1) Copy the S-TAP RPM from the Guardium Collector appliance: scp -P 16022 cli@<collector-ip>:/var/IBM/Guardium/stap/guard-stap-<version>-linux-x86-64.rpm /tmp/guard-stap.rpm (2) Install the RPM: rpm -Uvh /tmp/guard-stap.rpm (3) Write the guard.conf configuration: create /etc/sysconfig/guard.conf with contents: TAP_IP=<collector-ip>, GUARD_PORT=8075, DB_TYPE=<oracle|mssql|db2|mysql|all>, INSPECTION_ENGINE_COUNT=1, STAP_ENABLED=1 (4) Enable and start the service: systemctl enable guard-stap && systemctl restart guard-stap (5) Verify: systemctl status guard-stap. S-TAP communicates back to the Collector on TCP 8075.

question: How do you install S-TAP on a Windows database server?
answer: To install S-TAP on a Windows database server: (1) Copy the S-TAP MSI to the target server (e.g., C:\Windows\Temp\guard-stap.msi) (2) Run a silent install: msiexec /i 'C:\Windows\Temp\guard-stap.msi' /quiet /norestart GUARD_IP='<collector-ip>' GUARD_PORT='8075' DB_TYPE='mssql' (3) Start and enable the service: Start-Service 'IBM Guardium S-TAP'; Set-Service 'IBM Guardium S-TAP' -StartupType Automatic (4) Verify: Get-Service 'IBM Guardium S-TAP'. The MSI can be obtained from the Guardium Collector appliance or IBM Passport Advantage.

question: What is GIM and how does it differ from direct S-TAP installation?
answer: GIM (Guardium Installation Manager) is IBM's enterprise-scale S-TAP lifecycle management platform. Unlike direct SSH/WinRM installation where you manually deploy S-TAP to each server, GIM provides: (1) Centralised push deployment — send a REST API call to the GIM server (TCP 8082) and it pushes S-TAP to the target database server; (2) Centralised upgrade and removal management across all agents; (3) Health monitoring and status reporting for all S-TAP agents from a single dashboard; (4) Configuration push — update guard.conf settings across hundreds of servers simultaneously. GIM is recommended for deployments with more than 10 database servers. The GIM REST API endpoint for installation is POST /gim/rest/v1/installations with payload: targetHost, collectorIP, osType, dbType, guardiumVersion, installationType='STAP', autoStart=true.

question: What are the required firewall ports for IBM Guardium?
answer: Required firewall ports for IBM Guardium: TCP 8075 — S-TAP agent to Collector communication (must be open from all database servers to the Collector); TCP 8443 — Guardium REST API and Web UI (open from admin workstations and automation hosts); TCP 16022 — Guardium appliance SSH/CLI access; TCP 8082 — GIM (Guardium Installation Manager) server; TCP 9500 — Collector to Aggregator data transfer; TCP 16016 — Guardium internal communication between appliances. For the database servers themselves, no inbound ports are required for S-TAP — S-TAP initiates the outbound connection to the Collector on TCP 8075.

question: How do you configure network settings on a Guardium appliance via the CLI?
answer: To configure network settings on a Guardium appliance via the CLI (after first-boot NM_setup or via SSH on port 16022): (1) Set static IP and prefix: store network interface ip <IP>/<prefix> (e.g., store network interface ip 10.50.20.31/24) (2) Set default gateway: store network routes defaultroute <gateway-ip> (3) Set DNS resolvers: store network resolvers <dns1> <dns2> (4) Apply changes: restart network — then confirm with 'yes' at the prompt (5) Verify: show network interface all. These commands are the same on both Collector and Aggregator appliances. The NM_setup first-boot wizard provides an interactive menu for the same operations on first deployment.

question: What baseline security policies should be deployed on a Guardium Collector?
answer: Four essential baseline security policies for IBM Guardium: (1) BASELINE_AUDIT — audits all privileged DB user activity including DBA, sys, sa, root, postgres, admin accounts for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL, and EXECUTE operations; (2) PCI_DSS_AUDIT — audits access to cardholder data tables (card%, payment%, credit%, chd%) for all data manipulation operations, plus alerts on all failed login attempts (severity: CRITICAL); (3) HIPAA_AUDIT — audits access to PHI tables (patient%, phi%, medical%, health%) for all data access; (4) EXTRUSION_DETECT — alerts when any SELECT returns more than 1,000 rows, detecting potential data exfiltration. Deploy via POST /restAPI/policy (create), POST /restAPI/policy_rule (add rules), POST /restAPI/install_policy (activate).

question: What is Guardium Insights and how does it differ from Guardium Data Protection?
answer: IBM Guardium Insights is an analytics and risk intelligence layer built on top of Guardium Data Protection. Key differences: Guardium Data Protection (GDP) focuses on real-time database activity monitoring, policy enforcement, and blocking — it captures, inspects and reacts to database traffic in real time. Guardium Insights provides a higher-level analytics perspective: AI/ML-based anomaly detection, risk scoring across all data sources, compliance reporting dashboards (PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR, SOX), federated search across multiple Guardium environments, and integration with IBM QRadar SIEM. Guardium Insights can aggregate data from multiple GDP Collectors and Aggregators. It deploys as SaaS on IBM Cloud or on-premises on Red Hat OpenShift 4.x. Think of GDP as the enforcement layer and Guardium Insights as the intelligence and compliance layer.

question: What Guardium versions exist and what are the key differences?
answer: Key IBM Guardium Data Protection versions: GDP 11.x — uses RHEL 7 base OS, supports databases on Linux, Windows, AIX, Solaris, HP-UX; GDP 12.0/12.1 — transition to RHEL 9 base; GDP 12.2 — RHEL 9.6 base, updated isolinux installer menu (entry 1 = std/Collector, entry 3 = agg/Aggregator), improved REST API, S-TAP enhancements; GDP 12.2.2 — latest patch release with security fixes. Version 12.x introduces significant changes: the installer ISO menu order changed, requiring 0 Down arrow presses for Collector and 2 Down arrow presses for Aggregator before Enter during automated installation. Always verify the exact patch level when deploying S-TAP bundles as they are version-specific.

question: What is IBM QRadar SIEM and what are its main components?
answer: IBM QRadar SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) is an enterprise security analytics platform. Main components: (1) Console — central management UI, correlation engine, Ariel Query Engine for log searches, offense management; (2) Event Processor (EP) — collects and processes log events from data sources, communicates to Console on TCP 32004; (3) Flow Processor (FP) — collects and processes network flow data (NetFlow, sFlow, IPFIX); (4) Event Collector (EC) — lightweight collector deployed close to data sources, forwards to Event Processors; (5) Data Node — expands storage capacity. Key ports: TCP 443 (UI), TCP 32004 (EP-to-Console), TCP 514/UDP 514 (syslog), TCP 8413 (API). QRadar supports 450+ DSM (Device Support Module) parsers for normalising events from different sources.

question: What is AQL in QRadar and give an example query?
answer: AQL (Ariel Query Language) is QRadar's SQL-like language for querying events, flows, and assets. Example query to find Guardium policy violations in the last 24 hours: SELECT sourceip, destinationip, eventname, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM events WHERE LOGSOURCETYPENAME(logsourceid) = 'IBM Guardium' AND eventname ILIKE '%policy violation%' LAST 24 HOURS GROUP BY sourceip, destinationip, eventname ORDER BY cnt DESC LIMIT 100. Key AQL features: LAST <n> HOURS/MINUTES/DAYS time range, ILIKE for case-insensitive matching, LOGSOURCETYPENAME() function to filter by log source type, CATEGORYNAME() for event category names, QIDNAME() for event name lookup. Run via POST /api/ariel/searches then GET /api/ariel/searches/{searchId}/results.

question: How does QRadar integrate with IBM Guardium?
answer: QRadar integrates with IBM Guardium Data Protection via the Guardium DSM (Device Support Module): (1) Configure Guardium to forward audit events to QRadar via syslog in LEEF format (Log Event Extended Format — QRadar's native format); (2) In QRadar, the Guardium DSM auto-discovers or manually configured log sources parse and normalise Guardium events; (3) QRadar rules can correlate Guardium database access violations with other security events (e.g., network anomalies, authentication failures); (4) Guardium policy violations become QRadar events categorised under 'Database Activity'; (5) QRadar SOAR can receive QRadar offenses triggered by Guardium events and automatically open incidents. For Guardium Insights, a direct integration connector aggregates Guardium events into Insights analytics dashboards.

question: What is the QRadar SIEM REST API and how do you authenticate?
answer: The QRadar REST API is available at https://<qradar-console>/api/ and provides programmatic access to all QRadar functions. Authentication: (1) API Token — create a service token in QRadar Admin → Authorized Services, then pass as SEC header: curl -H 'SEC: <token>' https://<qradar>/api/siem/offenses; (2) Basic Authentication — pass Base64-encoded username:password in Authorization header. Key API endpoints: GET /api/siem/offenses (list offenses), GET /api/ariel/searches (list AQL searches), POST /api/ariel/searches (run AQL query with 'query_expression' in body), GET /api/config/event_sources/log_source_management/log_sources (list log sources), POST /api/reference_data/sets/{name} (add data to reference sets), GET /api/asset_model/assets (asset inventory). API version is passed as Version header (e.g., Version: 14.0).

question: What is QRadar SOAR and how does it work with QRadar SIEM?
answer: QRadar SOAR (formerly IBM Resilient) is IBM's Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response platform. It manages security incident response through automated playbooks. Integration with QRadar SIEM: (1) QRadar offenses automatically create SOAR incidents via the built-in QRadar SOAR connector; (2) Incident data flows bidirectionally — SOAR incident status changes update QRadar offense notes; (3) SOAR playbooks can query QRadar for additional context (run AQL searches, look up asset details). SOAR key concepts: Incident — a security event requiring response with phases, tasks, artifacts and timeline; Playbook — automated/semi-automated workflow; Function — Python-based integration performing an action (block IP, lookup threat intel, create ticket); App Exchange — pre-built SOAR integrations. SOAR supports MITRE ATT&CK framework mapping and provides SLA tracking for incident response timelines.

question: What is a QRadar offense and how does it differ from an event?
answer: In QRadar SIEM: An Event is a single normalised log entry from a data source (e.g., one firewall deny, one failed login, one Guardium policy violation). An Offense is an aggregated alert created when one or more correlation rules fire. Offenses group related events together to reduce alert fatigue and provide context. Key differences: Events are raw (normalised) data; offenses are actionable alerts. An offense has: a magnitude score (1-10 based on severity, credibility, relevance), a source IP, destination IP/network, contributing events count, and an assigned status (Active/Hidden/Closed). Building Blocks are reusable rule components that test conditions but do not generate offenses. QRadar Rules use AND/OR logic to correlate events, flows, and offense data. Rules can test: same source IP, same destination, time correlation, event count thresholds, and reference set membership.

question: What is IBM Security Verify Access (ISVA) and what does it provide?
answer: IBM Security Verify Access (ISVA, formerly IBM Security Access Manager / ISAM) is an on-premises or containerised access management solution providing: (1) WebSEAL reverse proxy — a Policy Decision Point (PDP) that intercepts HTTP/S traffic and enforces access policies; (2) Federated SSO — SAML 2.0, OIDC/OAuth 2.0, WS-Federation, JWT; (3) Step-up and risk-based MFA — TOTP, push notification, SMS OTP, FIDO2/WebAuthn; (4) OAuth/OIDC server — API protection and token issuance; (5) Session management — single sign-on across protected applications. Components: PDP (WebSEAL), PAP (Policy Administration Point / Local Management Interface for config), PIP (Policy Information Point — retrieves attributes from LDAP/AD). Deployment: hardware appliance, virtual appliance (OVA), Docker/Podman, Red Hat OpenShift.

question: What is IBM Verify and how does it differ from IBM Security Verify Access?
answer: IBM Verify is IBM's cloud-based Identity-as-a-Service (IDaaS) platform (SaaS, hosted on IBM Cloud), while IBM Security Verify Access (ISVA) is the on-premises/containerised appliance solution. IBM Verify provides: cloud SSO with SAML 2.0, OIDC, OAuth 2.0; MFA (TOTP, push, SMS, FIDO2); adaptive risk-based authentication; user lifecycle management; API access management. ISVA provides: on-premises reverse proxy and session management; enterprise federation with deep customisation; integration with on-premises LDAP/AD; compliance with strict data residency requirements. Key distinction: IBM Verify is for organisations wanting SaaS IAM without managing infrastructure; ISVA is for regulated industries or organisations requiring on-premises control of identity data. Both support federation with each other and with enterprise IdPs.

question: What is IBM Verify Governance (IGI) and what identity problems does it solve?
answer: IBM Verify Governance (formerly IBM Security Identity Governance and Intelligence / IGI) solves enterprise identity governance challenges: (1) Access Certification — periodic reviews where managers certify whether users still need their access; automates campaigns on schedule or risk-based triggers; (2) Separation of Duties (SoD) — detects and prevents toxic combinations of access rights that could enable fraud (e.g., a user who can both create and approve purchase orders); (3) Role Mining — analyses existing access patterns to suggest roles that reflect actual business needs; (4) Compliance Reporting — pre-built reports for SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley), HIPAA, GDPR audit requirements; (5) Role Lifecycle Management — request, approve, review, and revoke roles through governed workflows. IGI integrates with IBM Verify Identity (ISIM) for provisioning and with QRadar SIEM for suspicious access correlation.

question: What is IBM MaaS360 and what endpoints does it manage?
answer: IBM MaaS360 is IBM's Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform delivered as SaaS. It manages: iOS (iPhone, iPad), Android (personal and enterprise), macOS (Macs), Windows 10/11 (PCs and tablets), and ChromeOS devices. Key capabilities: (1) MDM (Mobile Device Management) — enrol, configure, enforce compliance, remote wipe/lock; (2) MAM (Mobile Application Management) — distribute apps, wrap apps for data loss prevention, manage app configurations; (3) MCM (Mobile Content Management) — secure access to corporate documents from mobile devices; (4) MaaS360 Advisor with Watson — AI-powered threat detection identifying anomalous device behaviour; (5) Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) — per-app VPN and conditional access; (6) MaaS360 Connector — on-premises connector for Active Directory/LDAP integration and intranet resource access. MaaS360 integrates with IBM QRadar via the MaaS360 DSM for security event correlation.

question: What is IBM X-Force and what threat intelligence does it provide?
answer: IBM X-Force is IBM's threat intelligence and security research platform. It provides: (1) X-Force Exchange — a cloud-based threat intelligence sharing platform where organisations can access and share threat indicators; (2) Threat Intelligence Feeds — IP reputation (malicious IPs, botnet C2, anonymisers), URL/domain reputation, file hash reputation (malware), vulnerability data (CVEs with CVSS scores); (3) STIX/TAXII 2.1 compatible feeds for automated integration with SIEM/SOAR; (4) QRadar Advisor with Watson — integrates X-Force threat intelligence with QRadar offenses using AI to map indicators to MITRE ATT&CK techniques; (5) X-Force Red — IBM's offensive security team providing penetration testing, red team exercises, vulnerability management, and attack surface management services. X-Force publishes the annual X-Force Threat Intelligence Index report documenting global attack trends.

question: What is IBM QRadar EDR and how does it work?
answer: IBM QRadar EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response, formerly ReaQta) provides advanced endpoint threat detection and automated response. Key differentiator: it uses a NanoOS hypervisor-level agent that runs below the OS kernel, making it tamper-resistant even against kernel-level rootkits. Capabilities: (1) Behavioural threat detection — ML models identify malicious behaviour patterns (process injection, credential dumping, lateral movement) without relying on signatures; (2) Automated response — automatically isolate endpoints, kill processes, quarantine files on high-confidence detections; (3) Threat hunting — interactive investigation with full process tree visibility, network connections, file operations timeline; (4) MITRE ATT&CK mapping — all detections mapped to ATT&CK tactics and techniques; (5) Bi-directional QRadar SIEM integration — EDR alerts become QRadar offenses; QRadar context enriches EDR investigation. Supports Windows, Linux, and macOS endpoints.

question: What is IBM DataPower Gateway and what security functions does it provide?
answer: IBM DataPower Gateway is a multi-protocol API security and integration appliance. Security functions: (1) API Security — OAuth 2.0 token validation, JWT validation, API key enforcement, mutual TLS (mTLS); (2) XML/JSON Threat Protection — schema validation, DTD threat prevention, JSON depth/width limits, content injection prevention; (3) Rate Limiting and Quota Management — protect backend services from abuse; (4) Protocol Mediation — REST↔SOAP, HTTP↔MQ/JMS conversion with security policy enforcement at each hop; (5) Encryption/Decryption — XML encryption/decryption, SSL/TLS termination and re-encryption; (6) Digital Signatures — XML Signature validation (WS-Security), JSON Web Signature (JWS). Deployment options: IDG hardware appliance, virtual edition (Docker, VMware, OpenShift), IBM Cloud. DataPower is the API gateway layer in IBM API Connect. Events integrate with QRadar via DataPower DSM.

question: What is IBM Security zSecure and what does it monitor?
answer: IBM Security zSecure is a suite of tools for IBM Z (mainframe) security: (1) zSecure Audit — automated RACF (Resource Access Control Facility) audit and compliance reporting; generates reports for SOX, PCI DSS, HIPAA from z/OS security logs; (2) zSecure Alert — real-time security event monitoring for z/OS; detects RACF violations, started task anomalies, suspicious TSO activity, and sends alerts to QRadar SIEM via the zSecure DSM; (3) zSecure Admin — automates RACF administration tasks (user provisioning, group management, policy enforcement) to reduce manual errors; (4) zSecure CICS Toolkit — CICS transaction security monitoring and administration; (5) zSecure Visual — graphical RACF administration for non-mainframe administrators. zSecure integrates with QRadar SIEM via the zSecure DSM, forwarding z/OS security events in LEEF format for correlation with distributed security events.

question: What is IBM OpenPages and what GRC capabilities does it provide?
answer: IBM OpenPages is an AI-powered Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) platform. Capabilities: (1) IT Governance and Risk Management — IT risk register, risk scoring, control testing, risk heat maps; (2) Operational Risk Management — loss event management, key risk indicators (KRIs), risk and control self-assessments (RCSAs); (3) Regulatory Compliance Management — maps regulations (SOX, GDPR, BCBS 239, Basel III, DPDP) to controls, tracks compliance status; (4) Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM) — vendor risk assessments, due diligence questionnaires, ongoing monitoring; (5) Internal Audit Management — audit planning, fieldwork, findings, and remediation tracking; (6) AI Integration — watsonx integration for automated risk classification, control suggestion, and natural language risk queries. OpenPages integrates with QRadar SIEM (security risk evidence) and Guardium (data risk evidence) to automatically populate GRC risk records with security findings.

question: How do IBM Security products form a defence-in-depth architecture?
answer: IBM Security products form a layered defence-in-depth architecture: (1) Perimeter / API Security layer — IBM DataPower Gateway enforces API security, rate limiting, and threat protection at the entry point; (2) Identity and Access layer — IBM Security Verify Access (ISVA) enforces authentication, MFA, and authorisation for users accessing applications; IBM Verify (SaaS) or IBM Verify Governance manages identity lifecycle; (3) Endpoint layer — IBM QRadar EDR (ReaQta) monitors endpoints for behavioural threats; IBM MaaS360 manages and enforces compliance on mobile/UEM endpoints; (4) Database layer — IBM Guardium Data Protection monitors all database activity in real time, enforces policies, and blocks violations; (5) Intelligence and Detection layer — IBM QRadar SIEM aggregates events from all layers, correlates them with X-Force threat intelligence, and generates offenses; (6) Response layer — IBM QRadar SOAR automates incident response workflows triggered by QRadar offenses; (7) Governance layer — IBM OpenPages tracks risk and compliance status, integrating evidence from all layers.

question: How does IBM Guardium integrate with IBM QRadar SIEM?
answer: IBM Guardium integrates with IBM QRadar SIEM through two primary mechanisms: (1) Guardium DSM (Device Support Module) — configure Guardium to forward audit events via syslog to QRadar in LEEF (Log Event Extended Format). In Guardium, configure a syslog destination (Setup > Tools and Views > Audit Process Builder > Syslog). QRadar auto-discovers the Guardium log source or it can be added manually with the IBM Guardium DSM. Events appear in QRadar under the 'Database Activity' high-level category; (2) Guardium Insights connector — Guardium Insights can push aggregated risk events directly to QRadar. In QRadar, you can then write rules such as: 'When a Guardium policy violation event is seen from the same source IP as a failed authentication event within 10 minutes, create an offense.' This correlation catches scenarios like credential theft followed by database exfiltration.

question: What is the LEEF format used by IBM security products?
answer: LEEF (Log Event Extended Format) is IBM's custom syslog event format, native to IBM QRadar SIEM. Structure: LEEF:2.0|<vendor>|<product>|<version>|<eventId>|<attribute1>=<value1>	<attribute2>=<value2>... Example from Guardium: LEEF:2.0|IBM|Guardium|12.2|PolicyViolation|devTime=Oct 11 2024 14:23:01	src=10.1.2.10	dst=10.50.20.31	usrName=sa	policy=PCI_DSS_AUDIT	sev=8. LEEF uses tab-separated key=value pairs in the extension. IBM QRadar's DSM parsers natively understand LEEF without additional configuration. In contrast, CEF (Common Event Format) is ArcSight's format. IBM products that emit LEEF: Guardium, ISVA, MaaS360, zSecure Alert, Verify. QRadar can also ingest CEF and standard RFC 5424 syslog.

question: What compliance frameworks do IBM Security products support?
answer: IBM Security products collectively support major compliance frameworks: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) — Guardium monitors cardholder data access; QRadar provides audit trails; OpenPages tracks control compliance; HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) — Guardium monitors PHI database access; MaaS360 enforces mobile device compliance; zSecure supports mainframe HIPAA controls; SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley) — Guardium + zSecure provide audit trails; Verify Governance enforces access certification; OpenPages tracks IT controls; GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) — Guardium discovers and monitors personal data; OpenPages manages privacy risk; Verify provides consent management; NIST SP 800-53 — QRadar use cases mapped to NIST controls; full IBM security stack addresses AU (Audit), AC (Access Control), IA (Identification and Authentication), SI (System Integrity) control families; ISO 27001 — QRadar, Guardium, and OpenPages together address ISO 27001 Annex A controls for information security; DPDP (Digital Personal Data Protection Act, India) — Guardium data classification and access monitoring; CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) — Guardium sensitive data discovery and access monitoring.

question: What are the steps to deploy IBM Guardium on VMware vSphere from an ISO?
answer: To deploy IBM Guardium on VMware vSphere from an ISO stored on a Datastore: (1) Upload the Guardium ISO to the vSphere Datastore — via vSphere Client (Storage > Datastore > Upload Files) or govc CLI: govc datastore.upload -ds=datastore1 /local/guardium.iso guardium/guardium-12.2.iso; (2) Create a VM using Terraform with the vsphere provider, specifying the datastore ISO path in the cdrom block (cdrom { datastore_id = data.vsphere_datastore.ds.id; path = 'guardium/guardium-12.2.iso' }), disk for the OS, and vmxnet3 NIC; (3) Boot the VM — the Guardium ISO provides an isolinux menu: entry 1 (std) = Collector, entry 3 (agg) = Aggregator; use arrow keys or automated key injection to select the correct role; (4) Wait for installation to complete (30-90 minutes); (5) Complete the NM_setup first-boot wizard on the VM console to set static IP, gateway, DNS, and hostname; (6) Run converge automation to wait for SSH and validate the appliance.

question: How do you deploy IBM Guardium on AWS?
answer: To deploy IBM Guardium on Amazon Web Services: (1) Obtain the Guardium VMDK from IBM Passport Advantage; (2) Upload to S3: aws s3 cp Security_Guardium_V12_2.vmdk s3://your-bucket/guardium/; (3) Import as AMI: aws ec2 import-image --description 'Guardium 12.2' --disk-containers '[{"Format":"vmdk","UserBucket":{"S3Bucket":"your-bucket","S3Key":"guardium/Security_Guardium_V12_2.vmdk"}}]' — requires vmimport IAM service role; (4) Monitor import: aws ec2 describe-import-image-tasks --import-task-ids import-ami-XXXXXXXX (wait for 'completed'); (5) Deploy with Terraform using aws provider with the imported AMI ID; create EC2 instance with m5.2xlarge (minimum), gp3 encrypted EBS root volume (300GB minimum), static ENI in the correct VPC subnet; (6) Configure security groups: allow TCP 8075 from DB subnets, TCP 8443 from admin IPs, TCP 16022 from admin IPs; (7) Complete NM_setup on the EC2 console after first boot.

question: What are common troubleshooting steps when a Guardium Collector is not receiving S-TAP data?
answer: Troubleshooting when a Guardium Collector is not receiving S-TAP data: (1) Check S-TAP service status on the DB server: Linux — systemctl status guard-stap; Windows — Get-Service 'IBM Guardium S-TAP'; (2) Verify guard.conf has correct Collector IP: cat /etc/sysconfig/guard.conf — confirm TAP_IP=<collector-ip> and GUARD_PORT=8075; (3) Test network connectivity from DB server to Collector: nc -zv <collector-ip> 8075 or telnet <collector-ip> 8075 — if it fails, check firewall rules; (4) Check S-TAP logs on DB server: /var/log/guard/guard.log (Linux) or Windows Event Log; (5) On Guardium Collector CLI, run: show tapconfig — lists connected S-TAP agents and their status; (6) Verify Collector is not at capacity: check disk space (show disk) and process health (show processes); (7) Check the database listener is on a port that S-TAP is configured to monitor — the DB_TYPE in guard.conf determines which ports are monitored.
